3
Which two quantities are both vector quantities?
A
displacement and distance
B
force and momentum
C
torque and time
D
weight and pressure

hints: Notice the question needs both quantities in the pair to have magnitude and direction, so test each word like distance, time and pressure for direction.
Connect force to its push or pull direction and momentum to $p = mv$, where velocity gives the direction.
Compare the second word in each pair: distance travelled, time elapsed and pressure exerted do not point in a direction, unlike momentum.
walkthrough: Recall the rule: a vector has both magnitude and direction, while a scalar has magnitude only.
Check displacement, force, torque and weight: each needs a direction, so they are vectors. Check distance, time and pressure: they are specified by size only, so they are scalars.
For the force and momentum pair, force acts in a stated direction and momentum is $p = mv$ where $m$ is scalar mass and $v$ is vector velocity, so $p$ keeps the direction of $v$.
Eliminate the other pairs because each contains one scalar: distance in A, time in C, and pressure in D.
Both members are vectors only for force and momentum. This is option B.

A.explanation: Displacement is a vector but distance is a scalar with magnitude only and no direction.

B.explanation: Force has magnitude and direction, and momentum $p = mv$ has the direction of velocity, so both are vectors.

C.explanation: Torque is a vector but time has magnitude only and is a scalar.

D.explanation: Weight is a vector force due to gravity but pressure $p = F/A$ is a scalar with magnitude only.
